title: You Think Brain Chips Control Thoughts, Yet Delgado's Bull Only Turned on Motor Circuits
description:
Experimental Chronicle — José Delgado (1965): Stopping a Charging Bull in Córdoba With a Radio 'Stimoceiver' — Fact vs Mind-Control Myth, grounded in José M. R. Delgado (1955) (Electroencephalography and Clinical Neurophysiology). Empirical findings show that before the 1960s, stimulating deep animal brain structures required thick overhead tether wires keeping animals strapped to lab benches. At Yale University, Spanish-born physiologist José M. R. Delgado invented the 'Stimoceiver' — a miniature FM radio receiver-stimulator small enough to sit cleanly on the skull with zero tether wires.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how motor cortex, basal ganglia, thalamus coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that in 1964 on a sunny afternoon at the La Alamiriya ranch bullring in Córdoba, Spain, Delgado stepped onto the sand wearing no sword — holding only a red cape and a small boxy handheld radio transmitter facing a charging 550-pound brave bull (Lucero) implanted in the caudate nucleus (basal ganglia) and thalamus.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- José M. R. Delgado (1955). Evaluation of permanent implantation of electrodes within the brain. Electroencephalography and Clinical Neurophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1016/0013-4694(55)90091-2
- Osmundsen, J. A. (1965, May 17). 'Matador' With a Radio Stops Wired Bull: Modified Behavior of Animals the Subject of Brain Study by Yale Scientist (José M. R. Delgado, Córdoba). The New York Times, p. 1.
- John Horgan (2005). The Forgotten Era of Brain Chips. Scientific American. https://doi.org/10.1038/scientificamerican1005-66

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.

offcenter_creator_bet: Honest take: Delgado's bull was overhyped — radio pulses steered motor turns rather than erasing inner anger. Where should medicine draw the line on neural steering?
